summary: Defines the Protocol to Access White-Space databases (PAWS). Unused slices of licensed radio spectrum can be used by others without interference. A device asks a database which frequencies are free at its location and time, and the database answers.

eli5.summary: Radio airwaves have empty gaps. Before using one, your gadget asks a map where it is and when it is free, so it does not bother the station.

questions: how does a white space database work
what is a master device in paws
what is a ruleset in paws
subtitle: How a radio device asks a database which frequencies it may use at its location, and for how long.

tldr.problem: Parts of the radio spectrum are licensed to primary users but often sit unused, and secondary devices need a standard way to learn where and when they may transmit without interfering.
tldr.mechanism: A device with geolocation sends its location to a spectrum database over HTTPS using JSON-RPC messages, and the database answers with a schedule of permitted frequencies and power levels under a named ruleset.
tldr.outcome: Regulatory complexity moves out of devices and into a few databases, and one protocol works across regulatory domains through registered rulesets. The database cannot force a device to obey the answer.

today: RFC 7545 is a Proposed Standard from May 2015, and the metadata for this site lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It defines PAWS, version 1.0, and leaves the actual rules to registered rulesets.

sections.title: White Space and Spectrum Databases
sections.content:
Portions of the radio spectrum allocated to licensees can be used by others without interference. This available spectrum is called white space. One way to manage such sharing is to have a geospatial database track available spectrum under the rules of one or more regulatory domains and report it to devices. RFC 7545 defines the Protocol to Access White-Space (PAWS) Databases for this.

The approach shifts the complexity of spectrum-policy conformance out of the device and into the database, and simplifies policy changes, because only a handful of databases need updating instead of numerous devices. To protect primary users, a database records information such as a fixed transmitter's call sign, geolocation, antenna height, power and periods of operation. Differences between regulatory domains should be handled by the database and hidden from devices as far as possible.

PAWS is an extensible protocol built on HTTP and TLS, for devices that have geolocation capability. Readers are pointed to RFC 6953 for use cases and requirements.
sections.eli5: Some radio channels are mostly empty, like a quiet lane on a road. A database is the traffic map that tells your gadget which lane is free where you are, so the gadget does not have to know every rule itself.

sections.title: Devices, Databases and Rulesets
sections.content:
A Master Device queries the database, for itself or for a Slave Device that asks through it. A Database holds current information about available spectrum at a given location and time. A Listing server provides the URIs of one or more databases, for example to publish the authorized databases of a regulator.

A regulatory domain is a place where certain rules for white-space use apply, normally defined by a government for a country. A ruleset is the set of rules governing white-space devices and databases. A ruleset can be identified by a registered ruleset identifier, normally naming the regulator and a version, such as FccTvBandWhiteSpace-2010. Supporting a ruleset means having out-of-band knowledge of its rules and conforming to them.

Separating the authority from the ruleset ID lets several authorities share a device-side ruleset and lets one authority define several rulesets. A device that supports several rulesets can list their IDs in its request, and the database replies with the applicable one, or with an error naming missing parameters so the device can try again.
sections.eli5: A master gadget is the one allowed to talk to the map. A ruleset is a rulebook for one country, with a name and a year on the cover so everyone knows which book is meant.

sections.title: The Protocol Steps
sections.content:
A typical session goes like this. The Master Device gets the URI of a suitable database, either preconfigured or from a listing server, and opens an HTTPS session. It may send an initialization message to exchange capabilities. The database may require registration before service. The device then sends an available-spectrum request containing its location, and the database answers with an available-spectrum response. The device may send a spectrum-use notification, which is purely informational and not a request for permission, and the database acknowledges it. Some regulatory domains require registration, slave verification or notifications.

Of the components, database discovery and the available-spectrum query are required, initialization is required for the database, and registration, spectrum-use notification and device validation are optional. A device must use initialization when parameterized-rule values are not preconfigured for the ruleset at its location.

The available-spectrum response contains, per ruleset, spectrum schedules: permissible power (EIRP) over time, with disjoint, sorted intervals. A gap means no spectrum is available. When the stop time of a schedule is reached, the device MUST get a new schedule, and if it cannot reach the database it MUST treat this as no available spectrum. A ruleset may also require a refresh when the device moves farther than a threshold distance, and the response can carry a maximum polling interval in seconds.

A Master Device can ask on behalf of a Slave Device by sending the slave's device descriptor and its own location in masterDeviceLocation. The optional batch request asks about several locations at once, and the optional device validation request lets a master check whether slaves may operate without a full query.
sections.eli5: Your gadget says where it is, the database says which channels are free there and until when, and the gadget must ask again when the time is up. If it cannot reach the database, it has to stay quiet.

sections.title: Messages and Parameters
sections.content:
Each message is a set of named parameters with a type and a REQUIRED or OPTIONAL marker. Key data types include GeoLocation (a point with uncertainty, given as an ellipse, or a region given as a polygon, using the WGS84 datum), DeviceDescriptor (identity and ruleset IDs), DeviceOwner, AntennaCharacteristics, DeviceCapabilities, and RulesetInfo (the authority, the ruleset ID, and values such as maxLocationChange and maxPollingSecs).

Spectrum is described by Spectrum elements: a resolution bandwidth plus profiles, each a list of frequency and dBm points giving the maximum permitted power spectral density. For example, the text says FCC regulation would need one specification at 6 MHz and ETSI regulation two, at 0.1 MHz and 8 MHz. When several Spectrum elements appear, each is a constraint the device must satisfy at once.

All timestamps are UTC in the form YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. Parameter names are case sensitive. The current PAWS version is 1.0, with the minor number raised when methods are added and the major number raised for incompatible changes. Unknown extra parameters MUST be ignored by the receiver.
sections.eli5: Every message is like a form with labeled boxes. Some boxes must be filled in and some are optional, and if a box has a label you do not know, you just skip it.

sections.title: Errors and Database Changes
sections.content:
Errors carry numeric codes. Examples: -102 UNSUPPORTED (the database does not support the device or any requested ruleset), -103 UNIMPLEMENTED (an optional feature is missing), -104 OUTSIDE_COVERAGE, -105 DATABASE_CHANGE, -201 MISSING (a required parameter is absent; the database lists the parameter names), -202 INVALID_VALUE, -301 UNAUTHORIZED and -302 NOT_REGISTERED. The range -32000 to -32768 is reserved for JSON-RPC errors.

If a database is unreachable or returns UNSUPPORTED, the device SHOULD pick another from its list. If none can be contacted, it MUST treat that as no available spectrum, though spectrum it already holds may be used while its data is still valid.

A database MAY change its URI, but beforehand it MUST announce alternates through a DbUpdateSpec in its responses for a minimum of 2 weeks before disabling the old URI. Devices replace their entry with the listed alternates. This is not meant for dynamic load balancing.
sections.eli5: If a map office is closed or cannot help, the gadget tries another office. If none answers, the gadget has to assume the channel is not free.

sections.title: JSON-RPC over HTTPS
sections.content:
Messages are encoded as JSON-RPC 2.0, with the restriction that the id MUST be a string. Method names carry the prefix spectrum.paws.: init, register, getSpectrum, getSpectrumBatch, notifySpectrumUse and verifyDevice. The RFC also gives example encodings of the init and getSpectrum methods and of a DeviceOwner vCard.

Transport is HTTPS. A request is carried in the body of an HTTP POST, which is the only method REQUIRED, and the response in the body of the HTTP response. Implementations MUST follow the best current practices of RFC 7525. The server MAY require TLS client authentication. A database MAY redirect with an HTTP 3xx response, and the device must authenticate the database before following it. The database SHOULD use 307 to ask the device to resubmit the same request elsewhere.
sections.eli5: The questions and answers are written in a simple, tidy format and sent through the same secure pipe web pages use, so nobody can read or change them on the way.

sections.title: Extensibility and Registries
sections.content:
PAWS is extended through three IANA registries, all using Specification Required with a Designated Expert: the PAWS Ruleset ID Registry, the PAWS Parameters Registry and the PAWS Error Code Registry. A ruleset ID is 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, underscore or period and SHOULD include version information. Parameter names are 1 to 64 characters, by convention lowerCamelCase. The initial ruleset registry contents cover FCC and ETSI rules.

The RFC says no extension should return sensitive device-specific information such as device information or logs. An appendix describes how listing servers can support database discovery.
sections.eli5: There are official lists where new rulebooks, new form boxes and new error numbers get written down, so everybody uses the same names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The database cannot enforce through the protocol that a device uses only the spectrum it was given, so a device can cause interference without asking. PAWS therefore does not try to protect against malicious use of white-space spectrum. The risks it does address are accuracy (receiving wrong availability) and privacy (interception of identifying data such as serial number and location, or unauthorized access to registrations and request logs).

The RFC relies on HTTP over TLS, assuming the PKI is not compromised, to assure the device it is talking to the proper database, and to protect messages from modification and eavesdropping. Static provisioning of trusted databases is the discovery method it covers. Device information, owner information and location could let a database administrator track a device and user over time, which needs out-of-band mitigation. Regulators should not require DeviceOwner information for mobile devices, and location should be only as precise as needed.

Client authentication is not required for core PAWS, although a regulatory domain may require it, because a malicious device can operate without contacting a database, and fraudulent spectrum-use notifications do not change availability answers in domains with established rules.
sections.eli5: The map can tell you where it is safe to play, but it cannot stop a naughty kid from ignoring it. So the protocol focuses on making sure the map is the real one and that nobody snoops on where you are.

viz.caption: A TYPICAL PAWS EXCHANGE (RFC 7545, SECTIONS 3 AND 4)
PAWS JSON-RPC METHOD NAMES AND THEIR MESSAGES

items.label: INIT_REQ / INIT_RESP
items.desc: Exchange capabilities and get ruleset parameters.

items.label: REGISTRATION_REQ / REGISTRATION_RESP
items.desc: Register the device where a ruleset requires it.

items.label: AVAIL_SPECTRUM_REQ / AVAIL_SPECTRUM_RESP
items.desc: Ask for available spectrum at a location.

items.label: AVAIL_SPECTRUM_BATCH_REQ / AVAIL_SPECTRUM_BATCH_RESP
items.desc: Ask for several locations in one request.

items.label: SPECTRUM_USE_NOTIFY / SPECTRUM_USE_RESP
items.desc: Report the spectrum the device intends to use.

items.label: DEV_VALID_REQ / DEV_VALID_RESP
items.desc: Check whether slave devices may operate.

items.label: UNSUPPORTED
items.desc: The database does not support the device or any requested ruleset.

items.label: UNIMPLEMENTED
items.desc: The database does not implement the optional request or feature.

items.label: OUTSIDE_COVERAGE
items.desc: The location is outside the database's coverage area.

items.label: DATABASE_CHANGE
items.desc: The database has changed its URI.

items.label: MISSING
items.desc: A required parameter is missing; its name is listed.

items.label: UNAUTHORIZED
items.desc: The device is not authorized to use the database.

items.label: NOT_REGISTERED
items.desc: Registration is required but the device is not registered.
